title: A disabled theatre troupe makes able-bodied people the discriminated minority — not to make you feel pity
dek: Yaoyao flips the entire social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a complaint — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework. Its value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.
who: People working in public welfare, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why integration can't rely on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission call-to-action at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is a widespread phenomenon
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives during holidays, her feeling was "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got her first computer, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. After getting the job she bought herself a wheelchair and left the house in it. Another visually impaired mother was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, saying "you can't see, you can't raise a child." For years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These oral accounts made Yaoyao realize that being unable to leave the house is not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair. When she moved, she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung things all over the front and back of their chairs and hauled load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she didn't have a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao said she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and only realized one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people don't even have a chance to meet, "you have no chance for integration at all." This was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
points.body: Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), directly reverses identities: a nuclear war turns most people into disabled people, who through technological modifications like electronic eyes and cochlear implants become new humans; the remaining few able-bodied people, because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war," become original sinners, marginalized by society. Yaoyao's logic was that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning all the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights able-bodied people have to fight for. She calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to keep his son from suffering again because of an able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw to cut off his son's legs, and ends up lying in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes bring out discussions about original sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner. His first reaction was confusion: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act? Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs; when it was Wang's turn to speak, he would pat once. Director Ma Yan said that abroad there are already forms of blind and deaf people performing on the same stage: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin said that he had been around deaf people since childhood, but back then he thought these were two kinds of people born with communication barriers, that "it was absolutely impossible for them to communicate," and that this barrier was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time subtitle screens, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors wear earphones on stage to cheat
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were actually "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them seamlessly on stage. The director had no way to assess this and only wondered why the visually impaired actors learned their lines so fast. Conversely, the director didn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing on the side, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign language. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

points.h: She received the Best Play award in the ICU
points.body: In 2024, Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, other groups' tables were empty — they were dressed up waiting for the awards — while only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won the Best Play award, the highest prize at the Nanjing New Theatre Festival, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. At the same time the news reached the ICU, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was specially invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first integrated disability play, becoming the only production in the "No Impossible" section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health condition and family environment, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favors boys over girls, and the last story is adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script because their life experiences were so similar — only the diseases differed. When asked if they would still choose to be born if given another chance, most in the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; but Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice.

points.h: The same question, Cai Cong and she give opposite answers
points.body: The episode contrasts the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born with the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired. When his wife was pregnant, many people advised them to get tests to see if the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong didn't want to predetermine that such a life was not worth starting just because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give the child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and debate around this choice persists. The question the episode poses is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?
